one_liner: New header-only C++20 vec<T,N> SIMD engine (scalar, AVX2, AVX-512) whose AVX2 dot kernels beat a naive scalar loop 13.9x.
what_it_does: Vectis provides basic_vec<T, N, Abi> (f32<N>, f64<N>, i32/u32/i64/u64) with masks, select, reductions and a small math set (rsqrt, rcp, clamp, lerp), where N lanes may span several registers or a padded partial register, plus an AoS-to-SoA container (soa_array) driven either by pointer-to-member layouts or, on GCC 16 with -freflection, by C++26 reflection. It is a new API in the shape of std::simd, not a drop-in for anything; the backend follows whatever -march the consumer passes. A separate optional layer offers hand-written GAS AVX2 dot, saxpy and sum kernels with intrinsics twins, which the README itself recommends not adopting.
how_it_is_fast: Explicit 256-bit (AVX2) or 512-bit (AVX-512) lanes with FMA, and above all the freedom to choose the floating-point reduction order: the benchmarked dot kernels keep four independent 8-lane accumulators, breaking the serial dependency chain that an IEEE-strict compiler cannot reassociate without -ffast-math. The README's own breakdown attributes most of the 13.9x to that reassociation (four scalar accumulators alone give 2.05x) and under 2.3x to width and FMA. Capability concepts remove operations a backend lacks (for example 64-bit multiply on AVX2) at compile time instead of emulating them.
when_to_use: Learning or prototyping explicit SIMD on x86-64 with AVX2: the code base is small, heavily commented, and its scalar backend is a bit-exact oracle you can test against.
Float reductions (dot products, sums) over L1/L2-resident arrays where an explicit multi-accumulator order is acceptable and -ffast-math is not.
Particle-style kernels over a handful of float fields that stay in SoA form across several passes and fit in L1/L2 (README: SoA 1.3-1.6x over AoS scalar there).
GCC 16 users who want AoS-to-SoA conversion generated from the struct by reflection without a field list.
when_not_to_use: Production code: the repository is a few weeks old (7 commits on 2026-09-20/21, 0 stars, version 0.1.1), and commit 76b4ecc, made the same day as the first code commit, fixed AVX2 mask factories that were wrong for 254 of 256 bit patterns plus a per-lane constructor over-read.
ARM or other non-x86 targets: there is no NEON or SVE backend, so the whole library runs its scalar path there.
Transcendental math (exp, log, sin, cos), int8/int16 lanes, gather/scatter or compress/expand: all absent.

Bandwidth-bound data (L3 or DRAM-sized arrays): SoA ties or loses to AoS (0.87-0.96x) and the vector kernels converge on memory bandwidth; AoS-to-SoA conversion costs 2-4x a kernel pass at large sizes.
MSVC builds (the CMake script rejects non-GCC/Clang compilers) or builds that pass no -march, which silently get the scalar backend.

integration.dependencies: none (optional GAS assembly object for the asm kernels; CMake 3.24+ for the package)
integration.min_toolchain: C++20, GCC or Clang (CI: g++-13 to g++-16, clang++-18 to 20); reflection path needs GCC 16 with -freflection
integration.platforms: x86-64 for vector code (AVX2 via -march=x86-64-v3, AVX-512 via x86-64-v4); scalar backend on aarch64 and macOS; asm layer Linux/ELF x86-64 only

gotchas: Harness flaw: bench_asm times each 100-1500 ns call individually with steady_clock, and the timed lambda dispatches by strcmp on the row name first (one strcmp for scalar, three for intrinsics and asm), so timer and dispatch overhead sit inside every row. At n = 1024 the 4-accumulator FMA kernel's floor is about 128 core cycles (about 41 ns at 3.1 GHz; estimate from 2 loads per cycle and 8 floats per load), so roughly half of the 107 ns is fixed cost. That makes 'asm ties intrinsics exactly' weak evidence and compresses the speedups at L1 sizes.

The cycles/element column is rdtsc ticks over the whole 21-run batch, timer calls included, divided by runs x elements; it is a batch average in TSC ticks (not core cycles on a powersave-governed CPU) and does not correspond to the min-of-21 ns column it sits beside.

The 13.93x headline measures the intrinsics/asm twins in kernels/asm_kernels.hpp against a single-accumulator loop, not the vec<T,N> engine; bench_simd.cpp measures the engine against an auto-vectorised scalar loop, but no numbers from it are published. The -ffast-math 6.9x row has no benchmark code.

The asm layer is enabled by default on any x86 host but uses ELF directives (.type @function, .note.GNU-stack) and the System V calling convention, and CI's macos-13 x86 job passes -DVECTIS_ENABLE_ASM=OFF; expect assembler or ABI failures on macOS x86-64 or MinGW unless you turn it off (inference from the source).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: EVE covers far more ISAs (including NEON and SVE) and operations, and the Vector Class Library has years of use plus SVML-style math functions, so either is the default choice; pick Vectis only if you want a small AVX2/AVX-512 engine you can read end to end, with compile-time capability concepts and reflection-generated SoA. Against marcelcases/simd it is a library rather than a set of example kernels.
verified_claims_summary: On the author's Intel i5-6500T (Skylake, powersave governor), a hand-written AVX2 dot_f32 over 1024 L1-resident floats takes 107 ns (min of 21) in both intrinsics and GAS assembly versus 1491 ns for a one-accumulator scalar loop (13.93x) and 679 ns for a four-accumulator scalar loop (about 6.3x, derived from page data), built with CMake Release at -march=x86-64-v3 with AVX-512 disabled and an unstated GCC version. No AVX-512 number exists, and the README attributes most of the gain to summation order rather than width.
status_note: Single-author Apache-2.0 repository created 2026-09-20 with 7 commits, 0 stars and no release, last touched 2026-09-21; its CI and sanitizer setup is unusually thorough for its age, but it should be treated as an experiment until it shows sustained maintenance.
